articles.title: Transplanted pig kidney works in US man's body for record 271 days
articles.summary: A man has lived for a record nine months with a transplanted pig kidney while waiting for a human transplant.
articles.content:
A kidney transplanted from a pig has worked inside a patient for 271 days – the longest on record, say US doctors.

Tim Andrews said the transplant gave him "hope" and spared him months of needing to go to hospital to have his blood filtered by a dialysis machine.

The team at Mass General Brigham hospital say their work shows pig organs can be used as a "bridge" until a human transplant becomes available.

But the pig organ eventually failed and was removed so Andrews needed a short bout of dialysis before a donor was found.

Doctors and scientists are exploring xenotransplantation – using organs from other species – due to shortages of organs for transplants.

In the US, around 100,000 people are waiting for a kidney while only 25,000 transplants occur each year. More than 7,000 people in the UK are on the kidney transplant list.

Andrews was told it could take seven years to get to the top of the list, but that people live only five years, on average, on dialysis.

"I had a little bit of a shortage of time… it becomes very depressing," he said.

But he described the idea of a pig transplant as "hope" and the "light at the end of the tunnel".

"Hope is the biggest thing, the chance to be free from the [dialysis] machine and live your life."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant medical breakthrough where a pig kidney successfully functioned in a human patient for a record duration, offering a promising bridge solution for patients awaiting human organ transplants. This advancement addresses the critical shortage of donor organs and has broad implications for improving quality of life and survival rates for thousands of patients worldwide.
articles.personality_title: Pig kidney works in man’s body for record 271 days, offering new hope
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people with kidney failure wait a long time for a human organ transplant. In the US, about 100,000 people need a new kidney, but only 25,000 transplants happen each year. People often rely on dialysis, a machine that cleans their blood, but it can be hard to live on for many years.

**What happened** – Doctors at Mass General Brigham hospital transplanted a kidney from a pig into Tim Andrews, a patient waiting for a human kidney. This pig kidney worked inside his body for 271 days, the longest time ever recorded. During this time, Andrews did not need dialysis and felt hopeful about his future.

**Impact** – This is the first time a pig kidney has worked so long in a human, showing that pig organs might help people survive while waiting for human donors. It could reduce the time patients spend on dialysis and improve their quality of life. This breakthrough may also help reduce the number of people who die waiting for a transplant.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue to study how to make pig organ transplants safer and last even longer. They hope to use this method as a temporary solution, or “bridge,” until a human organ becomes available. More tests and patients will help doctors understand how to make this treatment better.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A pig kidney worked in a man’s body for 271 days, showing that animal organs can help patients survive while waiting for human transplants.

articles.title: One immune switch may help drive aging across the body
articles.summary: Aging may be partly fueled by immune cells losing their ability to clear away damaged, inflammation-promoting cells. Blocking a single receptor restored that cleanup process in mice, reducing inflammation and helping their organs, muscles, and memory remain remarkably youthful.
articles.content:
Aging happens at different speeds from one person to another, but it eventually affects everyone. New research from Stanford Medicine, conducted in mice and human cells, points to a particular failure in the immune system that may help explain why.

The researchers found that tissue-resident macrophages, a type of immune cell that lives permanently within organs, become less able with age to dispose of another class of immune cells. That decline appears to contribute to aging throughout the body.

When the scientists blocked a single receptor on these macrophages, multiple organs in mice retained more youthful characteristics. The effects were seen in the brain, heart, skeletal and heart muscle, liver, spleen, bone marrow, kidney, and colon. The receptor normally responds to a hormone involved in inflammation and pain in both mice and humans.

Disabling the receptor specifically in tissue-resident macrophages also protected mice from several problems associated with chronic inflammation and aging, including frailty, excess fat accumulation and heart trouble. Cognitive decline was substantially reduced as well, according to Katrin Andreasson, MD, the Edward F. and Irene Thiel Pimley Professor in Neurology and Neurological Sciences.

"We've been trying to figure out why we age," Andreasson said. "Now we know at least one big reason for it."

The findings are described in a paper published in Science. Andreasson is the senior author, and Jessy Tan, PhD, an instructor in neurology, is the lead author.

The results provide new insight into the important role that chronic, body-wide inflammation plays in aging and its associated health problems. They also point toward a potential drug strategy that could slow age-related deterioration in organs and possibly extend the number of years people remain healthy.

How the Immune System Clears Aging Cells

Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells in the immune system and serve as some of the body's most important first responders. They are produced in bone marrow and then enter the bloodstream, where they patrol for bacterial, viral, and fungal threats.

When neutrophils encounter pathogens, they can release toxic substances and even destroy themselves, spilling long strands of biological material that form web-like traps around invading microbes.

These cells do not live for long. A neutrophil may survive for as much as 24 hours, although 12 hours is more typical. Roughly 90% of circulating neutrophils eventually arrive in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow, where other immune cells remove them.

That disposal process is especially important as the body grows older. In aging animals, most neutrophils that never encounter a pathogen quickly enter senescence, a dysfunctional state in which they can release harmful chemicals that damage nearby cells and promote inflammation.

Neutrophil numbers increase with age, and a growing proportion of them become senescent.

"Senescent neutrophils are killing our tissues," Andreasson said. "Clearance of these cells is essential for preventing chronic inflammation."

The Body's Cellular Garbage Collectors

Macrophages are responsible for much of that cleanup. These versatile immune cells fight pathogens, coordinate responses from other cells and release growth factors that help damaged tissues repair themselves.

They also remove dead and dysfunctional cells.

"They're the body's garbage collection crew. A lot of that garbage is defunct cells." Andreasson said.

A large share of that cellular waste consists of neutrophils, with roughly 100 billion of them needing to be cleared every day.

There are several kinds of macrophages. Tissue resident macrophages are unusually long-lived cells that settle into organs during fetal development. Once established, they remain in those organs throughout life and adapt to perform specialized jobs in each location.

One of their most important responsibilities is swallowing senescent cells. The new findings show that neutrophils are particularly significant targets. About 100 billion neutrophils are produced each day, and they begin showing signs of senescence only 8 to 12 hours after entering the bloodstream. (Neutrophils that haven't arrived at senescence yet but have lived long enough and seen enough to put out "kill me now" flags of surrender on their cell surfaces are fair game.)

The problem is that tissue-resident macrophages themselves deteriorate with age. Andreasson and her colleagues reported in a 2021 Nature study that these long-lived immune cells become increasingly vulnerable to inflammation as animals grow older. They can then contribute to that inflammation themselves.

An Inflammatory Signal Grows Stronger With Age

One important part of this process involves prostaglandins, hormones produced by immune cells. One of the five types, called PGE2, can affect cells in different ways depending on which receptors are present on their surfaces.

One receptor for PGE2, known as EP2, strongly promotes inflammation. Tissue-resident macrophages contain large amounts of EP2.

PGE2 production rises in response to infection, injury and toxic substances, including compounds produced as the body ages. The researchers' earlier work showed that PGE2 levels increase substantially over time. At the same time, tissue resident macrophages develop higher concentrations of EP2.

Together, those changes create a harmful feedback process. Increasing PGE2 activity repeatedly stimulates EP2 receptors on tissue-resident macrophages. The new study found that this stimulation weakens the macrophages' ability to engulf neutrophils.

As a result, senescent neutrophils begin accumulating in the bloodstream and tissues.

Previous research from Andreasson's group also showed that the energy metabolism of tissue resident macrophages gradually deteriorates with age.

"Once that starts, there's a steady decline in a macrophage's performance," she said.

The new work suggests that EP2 is critical to that decline.

"We've shown that when tissue-resident macrophages don't have EP2 on their surfaces anymore or when that receptor is plugged up by a drug, this decline doesn't happen."

Blocking One Receptor Protects Multiple Organs

To investigate the receptor's role more closely, Andreasson's laboratory engineered mice whose EP2 gene could be deleted at a time chosen by the scientists, specifically in tissue-resident macrophages.

Removing EP2 restored the macrophages' ability to dispose of neutrophils, reversing the disruption caused by PGE2.

The researchers compared younger normal mice, aged 6 to 8 months, which corresponds roughly to late adolescence or early adulthood in humans, with older normal mice, aged 23 to 25 months, which are roughly comparable to humans in their 60s or 70s. They also studied nearly identical older mice whose gene for EP2 had been deleted when they were 4 to 6 months old (their "teenage" years).

The team identified 71 blood proteins whose levels had changed significantly in normal older mice. Remarkably, 59 of those proteins remained at youthful levels in older mice whose tissue-resident macrophages lacked EP2. Many of the proteins came from the liver.

"The liver is one of the body's most tissue-resident-macrophage-enriched organs and a major contributor to aging-related changes in blood chemistry," Andreasson said. "It's the central organ determining the body's metabolic rate."

Normal old mice accumulated senescent neutrophils in the liver, spleen and bone marrow. Smaller increases were also observed throughout the many other organs examined by the researchers.

Older mice whose tissue resident macrophages lacked EP2 were different. Their organs maintained the lower neutrophil levels normally seen in younger animals.

The mice also appeared younger, leaner and more physically fit than control animals of the same age. They had less visceral fat and more muscle, and their performance on tests measuring the function of several organs matched that of young mice.

Memory, Strength and Inflammation Also Improved

Removing EP2 from tissue-resident macrophages reduced inflammation in the blood, liver, colon, heart, kidney and hippocampus (a brain region tightly tied to memory and navigation ability).

Older mice without EP2 also performed like younger animals on tests of speed, balance and forelimb grip strength.

Their memory remained stronger as well. They navigated mazes and remembered previously encountered objects almost as effectively as younger mice, while outperforming similarly aged mice whose EP2 receptors continued functioning normally.

Searching for a Drug That Can Target EP2

No approved drug currently exists that can selectively shut down EP2 activity, although several medications affect PGE2.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory pain medications reduce PGE2 production. Andreasson noted that this is the mechanism through which aspirin and related drugs reduce pain, fever, swelling, and redness (That's how aspirin and similar drugs reduce pain, fever, swelling, and redness, the "four horsemen" of inflammation.)

The difficulty is that these medications also interfere to varying degrees with other prostaglandins that perform important functions. PGE2 itself can also have beneficial effects when it interacts with receptors other than EP2.

Instead of broadly suppressing PGE2, researchers would therefore like to target the specific EP2 receptor responsible for the harmful inflammatory response.

To test whether that approach might work, the scientists gave otherwise normal 22-month-old mice an experimental drug that inhibits EP2 for two months.

The treatment brought both total neutrophil levels and the number of senescent neutrophils in old mice closer to youthful levels. Experiments in cell cultures also showed that aging reduced the ability of tissue resident macrophages to engulf and digest worn-out neutrophils, while the EP2 blocking drug significantly restored that ability.

Similar Changes Appear in Human Liver Cells

The researchers then examined a large database containing information about different cell types in young, old and diseased human livers.

They found patterns resembling those observed in the mice. Older human livers showed increased neutrophil accumulation, greater neutrophil senescence, declining tissue resident macrophage function and elevated EP2 activity. Those changes were even more pronounced in diseased livers.

According to Andreasson, this was the first time these changes had been observed in human cells.

Improving the body's ability to remove aging neutrophils could eventually offer significant therapeutic benefits.

"We need to develop a safe drug" that blocks EP2 without interfering with earlier processes such as PGE2 production, Andreasson said.

A researcher from the University of Munster in Germany also contributed to the study.

The research was funded by the National Institutes of Health (grants 1RF1AG080742, 1RF1AG070839 and P30AG066515), the American Heart Association, the Phil and Penny Knight Initiative for Brain Resilience (at the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute), Stanford University, the Arc Institute, and the Chan-Zuckerberg Biohub. Part of the work was conducted at the Neurosciences Preclinical Imaging Community Laboratory at the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough identifying a specific immune mechanism that contributes to aging and demonstrates that blocking a receptor (EP2) in tissue-resident macrophages can restore youthful function in multiple organs and reduce inflammation in mice. This discovery has broad implications for potentially developing drugs to slow aging and improve healthspan in humans, representing a meaningful advancement in health research with wide societal impact.
articles.personality_title: Blocking one immune receptor helps keep organs young in mice
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have been trying to understand why aging happens. A recent study from Stanford Medicine looked at how certain immune cells change as animals get older, which may explain some effects of aging.

**What happened** – Researchers found that a type of immune cell called tissue-resident macrophages loses its ability to clear out old, harmful cells called senescent neutrophils as mice age. These neutrophils cause inflammation and damage. The scientists blocked a receptor named EP2 on these macrophages, which restored their cleanup ability. This helped keep organs like the brain, heart, liver, and muscles healthier and reduced signs of aging in mice.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it shows a clear immune system process behind aging. By blocking just one receptor, multiple organs stayed youthful, inflammation dropped, and the mice stayed stronger with better memory. This finding opens a new path for developing drugs that could slow down aging by targeting EP2.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to create safe drugs that block the EP2 receptor without affecting other important body functions. They also found similar signs of this process in human liver cells, which means this research could lead to treatments for people in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Blocking the EP2 receptor in immune cells helps clear harmful cells and keeps multiple organs healthier, slowing aging in mice and pointing to new treatments for humans.

articles.title: Immune therapy engineered inside the body eases multiple sclerosis
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02765-1Results from a small trial suggest a modified virus can instruct the immune system to wipe out disease-causing cells.
articles.content:
Credit: Keith Chambers/SPL

Symptoms for sixteen people with multiple sclerosis or other autoimmune conditions improved after receiving a treatment that produced disease-fighting immune cells inside their bodies, according to results1 from a small clinical trial. Researchers say the results are exciting but the treatment needs to be tested in more people.

The latest trial, published this week in The New England Journal of Medicine, used a modified virus to transfer genetic instructions for making chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) on participants’ immune cells, known as T cells. The CAR T cells target autoantibodies expressed by B cells, another type of immune cell, which attack the body’s own healthy tissue in people with autoimmune diseases.

“This is a very exciting proof-of-concept study” for in vivo CAR-T-cell therapy, which is made inside the body, says David Simon, a clinician-researcher at the Charité — University Medicine Berlin. In vivo therapy is cheaper and faster to produce than is conventional CAR-T-cell therapies that are made in a laboratory, he adds.

Conventionally, CAR-T-cell therapies involve collecting T cells from a person’s blood and editing them in the lab to produce CARs. The tweaked cells are then reintroduced to the body. Ex vivo CAR-T-cell therapies are used to treat blood cancers, and clinical trials are under way for autoimmune diseases such as lupus.

Developing an in vivo CAR-T treatment for any disease is “a big achievement”, says Bing Du, an immunologist at East China Normal University in Shanghai. The results are good and comparable with those for ex vivo CAR-T-cell therapy, he says.

Dai-Shi Tian, one of the trial’s lead investigators, says the team was encouraged by the results. “The responses are promising signals, but they are not yet definitive evidence of efficacy or permanent restoration of immune tolerance,” says Tian, a neurologist at Tongji Medical College at Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan, China.

Immune reset

The trial involved people with multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune conditions, including those that cause weakness or inflammation of a person’s muscles, or in which the immune system attacks the brain, spinal cord and eyes. The participants received a single injection of the viral cells into their bloodstream and were monitored for about six months.

The team used a virus called a lentivirus, designed by biotechnology company Shenzhen Genocury Biotech in China. Last year, another CAR-T-cell therapy using a lentivirus was shown to effectively treat blood cancer2.

The team reported that following treatment, the participants generated more CAR T cells over time. These helped to deplete the number of B cells and levels of autoantibodies that attack healthy tissue. The team says the participants’ replacement B cells did not produce such autoantibodies, suggesting that their immune systems had been reset. The people with multiple sclerosis showed improved motor and cognitive function, as well as reductions in fatigue. Those with other conditions affecting their muscles showed improved scores for muscle strength and decreased inflammation.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant medical breakthrough in treating multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune diseases using an innovative in vivo CAR-T-cell therapy. This therapy, which engineers immune cells inside the body, has shown promising clinical trial results with tangible health improvements for patients. The impact is broad and meaningful for many people suffering from autoimmune conditions, and the article provides sufficient context and details about the treatment and its benefits.
articles.personality_title: New immune therapy shows promise for multiple sclerosis patients
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Multiple sclerosis (MS) and other autoimmune diseases happen when the body's immune system attacks its own healthy cells. Traditional treatments can be slow and expensive, and scientists have been looking for better ways to help patients.

**What happened** – In a recent small clinical trial, 16 people with MS or similar autoimmune diseases received a new treatment. This treatment uses a modified virus to change immune cells called T cells directly inside the body. These changed T cells then target and reduce harmful B cells that attack healthy tissue. The study lasted about six months and showed that patients improved in muscle strength, brain function, and fatigue.

**Impact** – This treatment is different because it happens inside the body, making it faster and cheaper than older methods that modify cells in a lab before putting them back in. The patients’ immune systems seemed to reset, producing healthier cells that no longer attack the body. This approach could help many people with autoimmune diseases by improving symptoms and reducing inflammation.

**What's next step** – Researchers need to test this treatment in more people to confirm how well it works and whether the benefits last long-term. If successful, it could become a new standard for treating MS and similar diseases.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have developed a new immune therapy that safely reprograms patients’ cells inside the body, leading to improved symptoms in multiple sclerosis and autoimmune diseases.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle thérapie immunitaire prometteuse pour les patients atteints de sclérose en plaques
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La sclérose en plaques (SEP) et d’autres maladies auto-immunes surviennent lorsque le système immunitaire attaque les propres cellules saines du corps. Les traitements traditionnels sont souvent longs et coûteux, et les chercheurs cherchent des solutions plus efficaces.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Lors d’un petit essai clinique récent, 16 personnes atteintes de SEP ou de maladies auto-immunes similaires ont reçu un nouveau traitement. Ce traitement utilise un virus modifié pour changer directement les cellules immunitaires appelées lymphocytes T dans le corps. Ces lymphocytes T modifiés ciblent et réduisent les lymphocytes B nuisibles qui attaquent les tissus sains. L’étude a duré environ six mois et a montré une amélioration de la force musculaire, des fonctions cérébrales et de la fatigue des patients.

**Impact** – Ce traitement est différent car il agit directement dans le corps, ce qui le rend plus rapide et moins coûteux que les méthodes classiques qui modifient les cellules en laboratoire avant de les réinjecter. Le système immunitaire des patients semble se réinitialiser, produisant des cellules plus saines qui n’attaquent plus le corps. Cette méthode pourrait aider de nombreuses personnes en améliorant les symptômes et en réduisant l’inflammation.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs doivent tester ce traitement sur un plus grand nombre de personnes pour confirmer son efficacité et la durée des bénéfices. S’il fonctionne, il pourrait devenir un nouveau standard pour traiter la SEP et les maladies similaires.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont créé une nouvelle thérapie qui reprogramme en toute sécurité les cellules des patients directement dans le corps, améliorant les symptômes de la sclérose en plaques et des maladies auto-immunes.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva terapia inmunitaria muestra avances para pacientes con esclerosis múltiple
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La esclerosis múltiple (EM) y otras enfermedades autoinmunes ocurren cuando el sistema inmunitario ataca las células sanas del propio cuerpo. Los tratamientos tradicionales pueden ser lentos y costosos, y los científicos buscan mejores opciones.

**Qué pasó** – En un pequeño ensayo clínico reciente, 16 personas con EM u otras enfermedades autoinmunes recibieron un nuevo tratamiento. Este usa un virus modificado para cambiar células inmunitarias llamadas células T directamente dentro del cuerpo. Estas células T modificadas atacan y reducen las células B dañinas que atacan el tejido sano. El estudio duró unos seis meses y mostró mejoras en la fuerza muscular, la función cerebral y la fatiga de los pacientes.

**Impacto** – Este tratamiento es distinto porque ocurre dentro del cuerpo, haciéndolo más rápido y barato que los métodos antiguos que modifican células en un laboratorio antes de devolverlas al cuerpo. Los sistemas inmunitarios de los pacientes parecen reiniciarse, produciendo células más saludables que ya no atacan al cuerpo. Este enfoque podría ayudar a muchas personas con enfermedades autoinmunes mejorando síntomas y reduciendo inflamación.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores necesitan probar este tratamiento en más personas para confirmar su efectividad y si los beneficios duran a largo plazo. Si funciona, podría convertirse en un nuevo estándar para tratar la EM y otras enfermedades similares.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos han desarrollado una nueva terapia que reprograma de forma segura las células de los pacientes dentro del cuerpo, mejorando síntomas en esclerosis múltiple y enfermedades autoinmunes.

articles.title: Magic-mushroom compound blocks a severe side effect of chemotherapy, in mice
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02744-6Study shows that psilocybin acts on nerves to prevent the painful condition called peripheral neuropathy.
articles.content:
Studies in mice suggest that psilocybin, one of the psychoactive compounds in magic mushrooms, could prevent the chemotherapy side effect called neuropathy.Credit: Victor de Schwanberg/Science Photo Library

For many cancer survivors, the triumph of remission is undercut by a debilitating side effect: hands and feet that feel as though they are constantly burning, prickling with needles or encased in ice. Now, researchers studying this condition, called neuropathy, in mice have identified an unexpected defence against it: psilocybin, the psychoactive compound found in magic mushrooms.

Just two doses of psilocybin administered before chemotherapy completely prevented mice from developing neuropathy. The condition affects as many as 60% of people treated with platinum-based cancer drugs, which are widely used to treat tumours of the ovary and lung, for example. The results, published today in Science, offer evidence that psilocybin could help to protect nerve fibres before chemotherapy causes lasting injury1 — which current approaches can’t effectively prevent or treat.

“This study pushes the needle beyond the canonical indications of psychedelics like depression, addiction, anxiety, PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder],” says study co-author Moran Amit, a surgical oncologist at the MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, Texas. “For the first time, we’re looking at pain,” he says. “And we’re actually showing a really significant efficacy not in treating that, but in preventing that.”

Neuron starvation

Platinum-based cancer drugs and other chemotherapies cause neuropathy by damaging some of the information-gathering ‘sensory’ neurons that extend into the skin’s outer layers. Energy-producing organelles called mitochondria travel long distances through these neurons to the cells’ tips in the skin, but some chemotherapies can disrupt that process. Depleted of energy, the neurons’ tips degenerate, dulling tactile sensation and sparking chronic pain.

Faulty mitochondria cause deadly diseases: fixing them is about to get a lot easier

To test whether psilocybin could ward off that breakdown, the researchers gave mice two doses of the compound before the animals received each of six rounds of chemotherapy over eight months.

In untreated animals, chemotherapy caused pain hypersensitivity, dulled their ability to feel sensations in their paws and led sensory-nerve fibres in the skin to wither. But psilocybin pre-treatment preserved normal paw sensation and nerve endings without diminishing the chemotherapy’s ability to shrink tumours, the authors found.

The authors’ strategy of administering psilocybin to prevent neuropathy, rather than trying to undo damage, is a “clever treatment approach”, says Joe Cichon, a neuroanaesthesiologist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.

No trip needed

The authors found that psilocybin stops nerve decay by activating specific receptors on sensory nerve fibres across the animals’ skin. Turning on these receptors triggers a series of reactions that eventually enlist motor proteins to keep mitochondria moving along the neurons. “That’s quite surprising — I wouldn't have expected psilocybin to regulate mitochondrial movement,” Cichon says.

These neuroprotective effects do not require a psychedelic trip: when the researchers tested tabernanthalog, a non-hallucinogenic compound that activates the same receptors, the animals received similar protection against sensory-nerve loss and pain hypersensitivity.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough where psilocybin, a compound from magic mushrooms, prevents chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy in mice. This side effect affects a large portion of cancer patients and current treatments are ineffective. The study offers hope for a new preventative therapy with broad impact on cancer patient quality of life, supported by detailed experimental evidence.
articles.personality_title: Psilocybin from magic mushrooms prevents nerve pain caused by chemotherapy in mice
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many cancer patients suffer from neuropathy, a painful side effect of chemotherapy that causes burning, tingling, and numbness in the hands and feet. This condition happens because chemotherapy damages the nerves that sense touch and pain.

**What happened** – Scientists gave mice two doses of psilocybin, a compound found in magic mushrooms, before each round of chemotherapy. They found that this treatment stopped the mice from developing neuropathy. The mice kept normal feeling in their paws and their nerve endings stayed healthy. Importantly, the chemotherapy still worked to shrink tumors.

**Impact** – This is important because neuropathy affects up to 60% of people treated with common chemotherapy drugs, and current treatments cannot prevent it. Psilocybin protects nerve cells by helping their energy parts, called mitochondria, keep moving inside the nerves. This discovery shows psilocybin might protect nerves without causing a psychedelic experience, opening a new way to prevent nerve pain in cancer patients.

**What's next step** – Researchers will likely test if psilocybin or similar non-hallucinogenic drugs can safely prevent neuropathy in humans. If successful, this could lead to new medicines that protect nerves during chemotherapy, improving life for many cancer survivors.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Psilocybin stops nerve damage and pain caused by chemotherapy in mice, pointing to a new way to protect cancer patients from a common and painful side effect.
articles.personality_title_fr: La psilocybine des champignons magiques empêche les douleurs nerveuses liées à la chimiothérapie chez la souris
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreux patients atteints de cancer souffrent de neuropathie, un effet secondaire douloureux de la chimiothérapie qui provoque des brûlures, des picotements et un engourdissement aux mains et aux pieds. Cette condition survient parce que la chimiothérapie endommage les nerfs qui ressentent le toucher et la douleur.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques ont donné à des souris deux doses de psilocybine, un composé présent dans les champignons magiques, avant chaque séance de chimiothérapie. Ils ont découvert que ce traitement empêchait les souris de développer la neuropathie. Les souris conservaient une sensation normale dans leurs pattes et leurs terminaisons nerveuses restaient saines. La chimiothérapie continuait à réduire les tumeurs.

**Impact** – C’est important car la neuropathie touche jusqu’à 60 % des personnes traitées par des médicaments de chimiothérapie courants, et les traitements actuels ne peuvent pas la prévenir. La psilocybine protège les cellules nerveuses en aidant les mitochondries, les parties productrices d’énergie, à continuer de se déplacer dans les nerfs. Cette découverte montre que la psilocybine pourrait protéger les nerfs sans provoquer d’expérience psychédélique, ouvrant une nouvelle voie pour prévenir la douleur nerveuse chez les patients cancéreux.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont probablement tester si la psilocybine ou des médicaments similaires sans effets hallucinogènes peuvent prévenir en toute sécurité la neuropathie chez l’humain. Si cela fonctionne, cela pourrait conduire à de nouveaux médicaments pour protéger les nerfs pendant la chimiothérapie, améliorant la vie de nombreux survivants du cancer.

**Phrase clé** – La psilocybine empêche les lésions nerveuses et la douleur causées par la chimiothérapie chez la souris, ouvrant la voie à une nouvelle protection contre un effet secondaire fréquent et douloureux du cancer.
articles.personality_title_es: La psilocibina de los hongos mágicos previene el dolor nervioso causado por la quimioterapia en ratones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchos pacientes con cáncer sufren neuropatía, un efecto secundario doloroso de la quimioterapia que causa ardor, hormigueo y entumecimiento en las manos y los pies. Esto ocurre porque la quimioterapia daña los nervios que detectan el tacto y el dolor.

¿Qué pasó** – Los científicos dieron a ratones dos dosis de psilocibina, un compuesto que se encuentra en los hongos mágicos, antes de cada ronda de quimioterapia. Descubrieron que este tratamiento evitó que los ratones desarrollaran neuropatía. Los ratones mantuvieron la sensación normal en sus patas y sus terminaciones nerviosas permanecieron saludables. La quimioterapia siguió funcionando para reducir los tumores.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque la neuropatía afecta hasta al 60 % de las personas tratadas con medicamentos comunes de quimioterapia, y los tratamientos actuales no pueden prevenirla. La psilocibina protege las células nerviosas ayudando a que las mitocondrias, las partes que producen energía, sigan moviéndose dentro de los nervios. Este descubrimiento muestra que la psilocibina podría proteger los nervios sin causar una experiencia psicodélica, abriendo una nueva forma de prevenir el dolor nervioso en pacientes con cáncer.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores probablemente probarán si la psilocibina o medicamentos similares sin efectos alucinógenos pueden prevenir de forma segura la neuropatía en humanos. Si tiene éxito, esto podría llevar a nuevos medicamentos que protejan los nervios durante la quimioterapia, mejorando la vida de muchos sobrevivientes de cáncer.

**Frase clave** – La psilocibina detiene el daño y el dolor nervioso causados por la quimioterapia en ratones, señalando una nueva manera de proteger a los pacientes con cáncer de un efecto secundario común y doloroso.
